Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verses 1–2:

Surah al-Layl

There is no disagreement that it has twenty-one verses. There is disagreement about whether it is Meccan or Medinan. The majority hold that it is Meccan, while ʿAli ibn Abi Talha said it is Medinan. It is also said that some of it is Meccan and some of it is Medinan. Likewise, there is disagreement about its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). The majority hold that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and this was narrated through sound chains of transmission from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas and others.

Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari, because "he had in the house of a hypocrite a palm tree, from which some unripe dates would fall into the house of orphans in his neighbourhood, and he would take some of them from the orphans. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to him: 'Leave it to them, and you will have in exchange a place in Paradise.' He refused, so Abu al-Dahdah bought it with his garden. He said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: 'I will give it to them in exchange for the palm tree that is in Paradise.' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Do it.' So he gave it, and it was revealed." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar, in a lengthier and vaguer form in which Abu al-Dahdah is not named, from Ibn ʿAbbas through a weak chain, as the Hafiz al-Suyuti stated explicitly.

Some scholars mentioned that His saying, may He be exalted, within it: ﴿And He will keep far from it the most righteous﴾, and so on, was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and they remained silent about anything else. It is reported from some exegetes that this is agreed upon, although some of the Shia claim that it was revealed concerning the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honour his face, and the explanation of what it was revealed about will come, Allah willing. When He, glorified be He, mentioned in the surah before it ﴿He has certainly succeeded﴾, and so on, He mentioned within this surah the qualities by which success is attained and those by which failure is incurred. Thus it contains a kind of detail of that, especially since He, exalted be He, followed that with some kinds of success and kinds of failure, and we seek refuge in Allah. So the One who speaks, Mighty and Majestic, said: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿By the night when it covers﴾, i.e., when it covers the sun, as in His saying: ﴿By the night when it covers it﴾; or the day, as in His saying: ( He covers the night over the day ); or everything that it conceals in general with its darkness. The thing sworn by, in all three views, is the entire night.

﴿And by the day when it appears﴾, i.e., becomes manifest by the removal of the darkness of the night, or becomes clear and uncovered by the rising of the sun. The first meaning fits when what is covered is the day or everything concealed, since both imply the existence of darkness. The second meaning fits when what is covered is the sun, since it implies the setting of the sun; thus the contrast between the two companion phrases is apt on that basis. The difference between the two verbs in past and future form has already been discussed. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read "tatajalla" with two taʾs, with the pronoun referring to the sun, and it was also read "tujalla" with a damma on the taʾ and a sukun on the jim, again with the pronoun referring to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verse 3:

﴿By Him Who created the male and the female﴾. That is: by the Mighty One of great power who created the two kinds, male and female, from among the animals characterized by this (distinction). It has also been said: from among the children of Adam. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Kalbi said: what is meant by "the male" is Adam, peace be upon him, and by "the female" is Hawwa' (Eve), may Allah be pleased with her. In either case, "ma" is a relative pronoun in the sense of "man" (alladhi/man). It was preferred over "man" because of the intention of the descriptive sense, as you have heard. It may also be a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) particle, but that is not the best reading.

It was also read: "wa-alladhi khalaqa" (and He who created). Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa-al-dhakara wa-al-unthā" (and the male and the female), and Ibn 'Abbas followed him in this, as Ibn al-Najjar related in Tarikh Baghdad through the chain of al-Dahhak from him. It is also attributed to 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others related from 'Alqamah that he came to Syria and sat with Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him. Abu al-Darda' said to him: "Where are you from?" He said: "From the people of Kufa." He said: "How did you hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾?" 'Alqamah said: "(He recited) 'wa-al-dhakara wa-al-unthā'." Abu al-Darda' said: "I bear witness that I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite it this way, but these people want me to recite: ﴿wa-ma khalaqa al-dhakara wa-al-unthā﴾. By Allah, I will not follow them."

You know that this is an irregular reading (qira'ah shadhdhah), transmitted by single narrators (ahad), and it is not permissible to recite by it. However, with respect to the one who heard it from the Prophet, peace be upon him, it has the status of a mutawatir reading, so we permit reciting it.

Tha'lab mentioned that some of the early generation (salaf) read: "wa-ma khalaqa al-dhakari" with the Ra' in the genitive (jarr), and al-Zamakhshari related it from al-Kisa'i. They explained this as an apposition (badal) from "ma" in the sense of "wa-ma khalaqahu Allah" (and what Allah created), i.e., "and the created thing of Allah: the male and the female." It has been said: it may also be explained as a case of imagining the verbal noun, based on "ma" being a verbal-noun particle, i.e., "wa-khalqi al-dhakari wa-al-unthā" (and the creation of the male and the female), as in the saying of the poet:

"Those who seek gifts circle around his doors, as the monk circles the church (bay'ah)"
with the Ra' of "al-rahib" in the genitive, by imagining the utterance of a verbal noun; i.e., like the circling of the monk around the church.

Surah 92, verse 4. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani):

﴿Indeed, your striving﴾ means: your efforts (masa'iyakum). For the verbal noun (masdar) in the construct form (idafah) conveys generality, so it is grammatically plural in meaning. Therefore it is described with a plural, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿are diverse﴾. For shatta is the plural of shatit, meaning scattered (mutafarriq). It is also permissible not to treat your striving as carrying the sense of plurality, and for shatta to be a feminine verbal noun, like dhikra and bushra, serving as the predicate of it, with an elided noun (taqdir mudaf) meaning "possessor of diversity," or by interpreting it as a descriptive adjective, meaning "scattered," or by making it the very essence of dispersion as an intensification (mubalaghah). In any case, the sentence is the answer to the oath, as Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qatadah. It is also permissible that the answer is elided, as has been mentioned more than once. The meaning of the dispersion of the efforts is their divergence in the recompense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verses 5–7:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿As for he who gives and fears [Allah]﴾ etc., is a detailed explanation clarifying their divergence and difference in that regard. It is also permissible that by their difference is meant that some seek the day that reveals itself, some seek the night that covers, some are aided by the male, and some are aided by the female; in that case the answer would be strongly suited to the oath. Yet its remoteness and weakness are not hidden.

The apparent meaning of "giving" (i'ta') is the spending of wealth, and for this reason Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning is spending his wealth in the way of Allah, may He be exalted. Qatadah said: the meaning is that he gives the right of Allah, may He be exalted, and its apparent sense is the financial rights.

﴿And fears [Allah]﴾, i.e., fears Allah, mighty and majestic, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Qatadah's saying in its meaning is: and fears what He has forbidden. In another narration: the prohibitions of Allah, may He be exalted. Mujahid said: and fears stinginess, and this, as you see, is far off.

﴿And affirms the best [reward]﴾, i.e., affirms the best word, which, as Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and others said, and which is related from Ibn 'Abbas, is: "There is no god but Allah." Or it is whatever indicates the truth, as some of them said, and the word of tawhid enters into it primarily. Or [it means] by the best religion, which is the religion of Islam. 'Ikrimah and a group said, and it is also related from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the recompense with replacement in this world together with multiplication. Mujahid said: Paradise. It was also said: the recompense in general. And it is more preponderant in my view that giving is an allusion to financial worship, fearing is an allusion to what encompasses all other acts of worship from doing good deeds and abandoning evil deeds in general, and affirming the best is an allusion to faith in tawhid, or to what encompasses it and other things that must be believed in; and this is a detailed explanation comprehensive of all endeavors. The mention of giving first is because it is the apparent cause of revelation; for al-Hakim narrated it and declared it sound, from 'Amir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, who said: Abu Quhafah said to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "I see you freeing weak slaves. Why do you not, when you do what you do, free strong men who would protect you and stand before you?" He said: "O father, I only want what I want." So there was revealed: ﴿As for he who gives and fears﴾ up to: ﴿and no one has any favor with him to be repaid﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Abu Bakr bought Bilal from Umayyah ibn Khalaf for a cloak and ten uqiyya, and freed him, whereupon Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾. The same applies on the view that they were revealed concerning Abu al-Dahdah. Since faith is a matter given importance in itself, it was placed after fearing [Allah], so that its mention after it would be from the category of mentioning the particular after the general, along with what that entails of observing the rhyme (fasilah).

It was also said: the intended meaning is that he gives obedience, fears disobedience, and affirms the word that indicates the truth, such as the word of tawhid. But in this there is an objection: what is well known in "giving" is its connection to wealth in particular, especially since it stands in contrast to the mention of stinginess and wealth; and the matter of placing faith after it remains as it is. It was also said: it was placed later because among the components of giving obedience is listening in order to learn the word of tawhid, without which faith is not complete. And among the components of fearing [Allah] is guarding against associating partners, and both of these precede that; and this is not a valid point.

﴿So We will ease him toward ease﴾: i.e., We will prepare him for the state that leads to ease and comfort, such as entering Paradise and its beginnings, from the ease of a horse for riding when one saddles it and bridles it. He described it as "ease" either by explicit metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah), or by metonymy (majaz mursal), or by figurative attribution in the predication (tajawwuz fi al-isnad).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 92, verses 8–10:**

﴿As for he who is niggardly﴾ with his wealth, and does not spend it in the way of good. It is also said: that is, he is niggardly in doing what he was commanded, and there is much to say about this.

﴿And considers himself self-sufficient﴾: that is, he is indifferent to what is with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as if he were independent of Him, glorified is He, and so he does not guard himself against Him, exalted and high is He. Or, he is self-sufficient through the desires of this world, having no need for the bliss of the Hereafter. This is because it stands in contrast to ﴿and is mindful [of Allah]﴾. Just as the saying of the Exalted, ﴿and denies the best [reward]﴾, stands in contrast to ﴿and affirms the best [reward]﴾. The meaning of "the best" here is what has passed in the sayings before this.

﴿So We will ease him toward the difficult﴾: that is, toward the state that leads to hardship and severity, such as entering the Fire and its beginnings. He described it as "difficult" in the manner already mentioned. The root meaning of *taysir* (facilitation) is from *yusr* (ease), in the sense of smoothness, but what is intended here is preparation and readying for the matter, namely that which leads to comfort and that which leads to severity. As for the *sin* in ﴿fa-sanuyassiruhu﴾ (so We will ease him), it is said to be for emphasis, and it is said to indicate that the promised reward, most of which will occur in the Hereafter, is a matter awaited and deferred. The priority given to niggardliness, then self-sufficiency, then denial, is understood from what has preceded. In al-Irshad (the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud) it is said: perhaps the opening of the two categories with giving and niggardliness, although each of them is of a lower rank than what follows in terms of being followed by facilitation toward ease and hardship toward difficulty, is to indicate that each of them is the root of what follows them, namely affirmation and piety, and denial and self-sufficiency.

It is also said: facilitation in the first instance means divine favour (*lutf*), and in the second instance means abandonment (*khidhlan*), and "ease" and "difficulty" mean obedience, because it is the easiest thing for the one who is mindful of Allah and the most difficult for others. The meaning is: as for he who gives, We will show him favour and grant him success, until obedience becomes for him the easiest and least burdensome of matters, from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam﴾. ﴿And as for he who is niggardly,﴾ and so on, ﴿We will abandon him and withhold from him favour, until obedience becomes for him the most difficult thing and the most severe,﴾ from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾. The origin of this is: "So We will ease him toward the difficult obedience," and then what has been mentioned was intended, with the attribute itself being the object of the facilitation, namely the difficulty, not the thing described, namely obedience. Nevertheless, the use of "facilitation" with "the difficult" is by way of *mushakalah* (rhetorical correspondence of wording).

It is also permissible that "the ease" means the path to Paradise, and "the difficulty" means the path to the Fire, and that "facilitation" in both places means guidance, which in the Hereafter is promise and threat, and the rule of *mushakalah* remains as it is in this case. It is also permissible that facilitation means preparation and readying, and "ease" and "difficulty" mean obedience and disobedience, along with their beginnings from praiseworthy and blameworthy attributes. This is a good view, not far from the first, and both are a fine *tibaq* (antithesis), in accordance with what is authentically reported in the traditions.

Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at a funeral, and he said: 'There is none among you but that his seat in Paradise and his seat in the Fire have been written.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, should we not then rely [on that]?' He said: 'Act, for each is facilitated toward that for which he was created. As for he who is of the people of happiness, he will be facilitated toward the deeds of the people of happiness, and as for he who is of the people of wretchedness, he will be facilitated toward the deeds of the people of wretchedness.' Then he (ﷺ) recited: ﴿As for he who gives and is mindful [of Allah]﴾, the two verses."

The sum of what the Prophet (ﷺ) intended by his saying "Act," and so on, is: upon you is the affair of servitude and what you were created for and commanded with, and leave the hidden affairs of Lordship to their Owner, so there is no burden upon you concerning them. **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 92, verses 8–10:**

﴿As for he who is niggardly﴾ with his wealth, and does not spend it in the way of good. It is also said: that is, he is niggardly in doing what he was commanded, and there is much to say about this.

﴿And considers himself self-sufficient﴾: that is, he is indifferent to what is with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as if he were independent of Him, glorified is He, and so he does not guard himself against Him, exalted and high is He. Or, he is self-sufficient through the desires of this world, having no need for the bliss of the Hereafter. This is because it stands in contrast to ﴿and is mindful [of Allah]﴾. Just as the saying of the Exalted, ﴿and denies the best [reward]﴾, stands in contrast to ﴿and affirms the best [reward]﴾. The meaning of "the best" here is what has passed in the sayings before this.

﴿So We will ease him toward the difficult﴾: that is, toward the state that leads to hardship and severity, such as entering the Fire and its beginnings. He described it as "difficult" in the manner already mentioned. The root meaning of *taysir* (facilitation) is from *yusr* (ease), in the sense of smoothness, but what is intended here is preparation and readying for the matter, namely that which leads to comfort and that which leads to severity. As for the *sin* in ﴿fa-sanuyassiruhu﴾ (so We will ease him), it is said to be for emphasis, and it is said to indicate that the promised reward, most of which will occur in the Hereafter, is a matter awaited and deferred. The priority given to niggardliness, then self-sufficiency, then denial, is understood from what has preceded. In al-Irshad (the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud) it is said: perhaps the opening of the two categories with giving and niggardliness, although each of them is of a lower rank than what follows in terms of being followed by facilitation toward ease and hardship toward difficulty, is to indicate that each of them is the root of what follows them, namely affirmation and piety, and denial and self-sufficiency.

It is also said: facilitation in the first instance means divine favour (*lutf*), and in the second instance means abandonment (*khidhlan*), and "ease" and "difficulty" mean obedience, because it is the easiest thing for the one who is mindful of Allah and the most difficult for others. The meaning is: as for he who gives, We will show him favour and grant him success, until obedience becomes for him the easiest and least burdensome of matters, from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam﴾. ﴿And as for he who is niggardly,﴾ and so on, ﴿We will abandon him and withhold from him favour, until obedience becomes for him the most difficult thing and the most severe,﴾ from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾. This is a good view, not far from the first, and both are a fine *tibaq* (antithesis), in accordance with what is authentically reported in the traditions.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verse 11:

﴿And his wealth will not avail him﴾, i.e., it will not avail him. Whether "mā" is a negation, meaning "and nothing will avail him," or an interrogative, meaning "what will avail him," his wealth which he withholds [in stinginess].

Page 150

﴿when he falls [to ruin]﴾, i.e., when he perishes. The verb is taraddā, of the form tafa"ala, from al-radā, which is destruction (al-halāk), as stated by Mujahid. It was also said: he falls into the pit of the grave.

Qatadah and Abu Salih said: he falls into Jahannam, i.e., he plunges down. Others said: he falls in his shroud, from al-ridā' (the garment), and this is a metaphor for his death and destruction.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what precedes it; that is: indeed, upon Us, in accordance with Our decree, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdom, since We created creation for worship; that is, We show them and guide them to the truth. Or [it means] that We make clear to them the path of guidance and what leads to it, and the path of misguidance and what leads to it. And We have done that without anyone being able to compel Us. Therefore, the verse does not establish, in the sense claimed by the Mu'tazilah, that it is obligatory upon Him, Mighty and Majestic, [to guide].

It has also been said: the meaning is that guidance is entrusted to Us and not to anyone else, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills.﴾ The meaning is not that guidance is obligatory upon Us, such that its apparent sense would be evidence for the obligation upon Him (exalted is He above that by a great exaltation) of what is best (al-aslah). In this there is that the attachment of the preposition to the specific verbal-sense term (al-kawn al-khass), namely "entrusted" (mawkulan), is contrary to the apparent meaning. Similar to this is what has been said: the intended meaning is "Then indeed upon Us is the way of guidance," in the sense that whoever follows the way explained by guidance and by the direction towards it reaches Us. As has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon God is the direction of the path﴾, that is: whoever follows the straight, moderate path reaches Him, glorified is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verse 13:

﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ That is, to Us belongs complete disposal over both, in whatever way We will, so We do with them whatever We will of the acts, among which is what we mentioned regarding the one who gives and the one who withholds. Or it means that to Us belongs all of that, so We reward whoever is guided. And Our guidance is most effective in this. Or it means that to Us belongs everything in the two abodes, so your abandoning guidance and your not benefiting from Our guidance does not harm Us, just as your going astray does not harm Us; and your being guided does not benefit Us. So whoever is guided, he is guided only for his own self, and whoever goes astray, he goes astray only to its detriment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verses 14–16:

﴿So I have warned you of a Fire blazing fiercely.﴾ It is said: this is a consequence of the guidance being upon Him, glory be to Him; that is, "So I guided you by warning, and I went to great lengths in guiding you." And "tala" (blazing) means "taltahib" (flaming), and its origin is "tatalaza" with two tā's, one of which was elided. Ibn al-Zubayr, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Talha, Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr recited it that way. ﴿None will enter it except the most wretched.﴾ What is meant by it is the disbeliever, for he is more wretched than the sinner. This is made clear by His description of him, ﴿who denied﴾, that is, the truth, ﴿and turned away﴾ and withdrew from obedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verse 17:

﴿And he will be kept far from it﴾, i.e., the one who is most God-fearing will be kept far from it.

﴿The most God-fearing (al-atqa)﴾: the one who goes to great lengths in guarding against disbelief and sins, so that he does not even come close to it. It has been raised as an objection that burning in the Fire (salY al-nar) means entering it, or enduring its heat, and on the prevailing view this is a necessary consequence of entering it. Thus the restriction stated earlier (that only the most wretched will burn in it) requires that the believer who commits sins does not burn in the Fire, since he is not included in the general category of "the most wretched" described by what was mentioned. Also, "he will be kept far from it, the most God-fearing" implies by its inference (mafhum) that whoever is not the most God-fearing, namely the one who is God-fearing in a general sense, which is the believer who commits sins, will not be kept far from it but will burn in it.

So there is a contradiction between the two restrictions. The answer is that burning (salY) is not simply entering the Fire, nor simply enduring its heat, but enduring it in its most intense form. Ibn al-Munayyir reported from the leading lexicographers that salY means that people dig a pit, fill it with a large quantity of embers, and then deliberately push a sheep into the middle of it, among its layers. The meaning is therefore: no one is tormented among its layers and endures its heat in the most intense manner except the most wretched, and the most God-fearing will be kept far from it, so he does not enter it, let alone endure that. It follows from the first that whoever is not the most wretched, namely the believer who commits sins, is not tormented among its layers and does not endure its heat in the most intense manner. It does not follow from this that he will not enter it or be tormented by it at all. It is possible that he enters it and is tormented by it in its ordinary form, at a lesser degree than that torment. From the second it follows that whoever is not the most God-fearing is not kept far from it, but it does not follow from this that whoever else, namely the God-fearing in a general sense, which is the believer who commits sins, burns in it and is tormented among its layers with the greatest torment. Rather, its farthest implication is that he is not kept far from it, so it is possible that he enters it and is tormented by it in its ordinary form, not in its most intense form. Thus there is no contradiction between the two restrictions. Some scholars took the intensity to be part of the meaning of salY for the reason mentioned, and the necessity here is due to its being paired with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he will be kept far from it﴾. So it is said.

It has been deemed good to make the sin (sin) in al-sa-yuj-annabuha into an emphatic particle (lil-ta'kid, for emphasis), so that the meaning becomes: "the most God-fearing will certainly be kept far from it." On the view that implication (mafhum) is valid, this indicates that whoever is other than him, namely the believer who commits sins,
[p. 151]
will not be kept far from it, and this is certain, in the sense that it is permissible that he be kept far from it, and it is permissible that he not be kept far from it but enter it without burning in it.

Al-Zamakhshari stated the objection as follows: it is known that every wretched person burns in it, and every God-fearing person is kept far from it. Burning is not restricted to the most wretched of the wretched, nor is being kept far and salvation restricted to the most God-fearing of the God-fearing, and the apparent meaning of the two sentences is that. He answered with what amounts to this: where the verse comes in order to compare two states, one of a great man among the polytheists and one of a great man among the believers, the restriction is a claim made for emphasis, not a literal one. Had this not been the most wretched, he would not have been unburnt, and had this not been the most God-fearing, he would not have been kept entirely far from it. Al-Kashshaf praised this and said: "It is a fine meaning. You know that the basis of what he said is Mu'tazilism (i'tizal) and the eternal punishment of sinners in the Fire."

Al-Qadi said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿he will not burn in it﴾ does not indicate that He, exalted is He, will not cause anyone to enter the Fire except the disbelievers, as the Murji'ah say. This is because He, exalted is He, made "the Fire" indefinite (nakkara al-nar), so what is meant is that a fire among the fires will not be burned in except by one whose state is this, and the Fire has levels (darakat), as is known from the verses. So from where is it known that this particular Fire will not be burned in by other people?

Al-Zamakhshari responded to this: what can be done about His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the most God-fearing will be kept far from it﴾? For it is known that the most sinful of the Muslims is kept far from that specific Fire, not only the most God-fearing among them. It was answered that perhaps this speaker does not hold the view of the implication of a descriptive attribute (mafhum al-sifah) and the like, so the verse does not, in his view, indicate restriction. The distinction of this most God-fearing one in his view comes from the totality of being kept far together with what will be mentioned afterwards. Perhaps everyone who does not hold the view of implication is only troubled by the matter of the restriction in: "he will not burn in it..." etc., for it is in appearance like an explicit text regarding what the Murji'ah claim, since they understand burning in it as merely entering it. They supported this with what Imam Ahmad, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "None enters the Fire except the one who is wretched." It was said: "And who is the wretched one?" He said: "The one who does not perform any obedience to God, exalted is He, and does not abandon any disobedience to God, exalted is He."

This report and others like it are among the reports they rely on to establish their claim. The People of the Sunnah interpret whatever of such reports is authentic in light of the texts that indicate the punishment of some who committed major sins, as explained in its proper place. It has also been said in reply that the intended meaning of "the most wretched" and "the most God-fearing" is "the wretched" and "the God-fearing," and the form af'al (superlative) was common in such usage. From this is the saying of Tarafa:

"Men wished that I would die, and if I die, that is a path in which I am not the only one."

He meant by "wahid" (single, unique) ... It was objected that this does not resolve the problem of the objection, since the "wretched" in the verse is none other than the disbeliever, so the restriction would require that no one other than him enter the Fire or be tormented in it, and this contradicts the true doctrine. Also, that God-fearing one has been described with what he has been described with, so on the view of implication it would follow that a God-fearing person who is not described by that, such as one who has no wealth, and others, and children and the insane who are not legally responsible, would not be kept far from it. Yet the truth is that they keep away from it. It has been said otherwise. Perhaps, after you have become acquainted with this, carefully examined everything that has been said, and recalled what the community holds among those who have knowledge of the consensus (ahl al-jam'), you will find it good, if you hold the view of implication, what Sahib al-Kashf found good from what has passed from al-Zamakhshari. But if you are not one who holds that the people of major sins among the believers are eternally punished, then reflect.

The verb jannaba takes two objects. So the pronoun "ha" here is the second object, and "al-atqa" is the first object, which is the deputy of the subject (na'ib 'an al-fa'il). It is said: "So-and-so was kept from good" (junniba fulan khayran), and "was kept from evil" (junniba sharran), and when used without a complement one says: "So-and-so was kept away" (junniba fulan). Its meaning, according to al-Raghib, is: he was distanced from good. The root meaning of jannabtuhu, as it has been said, is: I placed him on one of its sides. It is often used to mean causing distance, and this is the case here. For this reason we said: that is, he will be kept far from it, the most God-fearing one.

﴿Who gives his wealth﴾, i.e., gives it and spends it, ﴿seeking to purify himself﴾, desiring that he be, in the sight of Allah the Exalted, one who grows and increases [in reward], not intending by it ostentation (*riya'*) or reputation (*sum'ah*); or [seeking to be] purified from sins. So the clause is in the accusative (*nasb*) as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yu'ti*. It is permitted that it be a substitute (*badal*) for the relative clause (*sila*), in which case it has no place in grammatical inflection (*i'rab*). It is also permitted that the verb alone be a substitute for the preceding verb alone. Both possibilities are objected to on the grounds that the substitute belongs to the category of the follower (*tabi'*), defined as "every second [word] that takes the *i'rab* of its predecessor," and a relative clause has no *i'rab* such that a follower could acquire it. The cause of the *i'rab* in the verb, which is *raf'* (nominative), is present regardless of the following, and according to the well-known view it is the verb's being free of the governing particle (*nasib*) and the apocopating particle (*jazm*). Therefore it is not inflected with the *i'rab* of its predecessor, because it is evident that the *i'rab* of a follower is due to following, whereas here the *raf'* is not due to that but due to being free [of the governing and apocopating particles].

It was answered, setting aside what is in that definition, some of which al-Radi has pointed out: as for the first objection, the intended meaning is "takes the *i'rab* of its predecessor if it has *i'rab*," or the intended meaning is "takes the *i'rab* of its predecessor in existence and in non-existence." It was said that applying the term "follower" to that and similar cases, such as the particle or the verb that is not inflected, is metaphorical, insofar as it resembles a follower in agreeing with its predecessor in what it has. As for the second objection, the answer is that a thing may be intended for one purpose even if it is already established before that purpose for another reason, like the *alif* of the dual (*alif al-tathniyah*) and the *waw* of the plural (*waw al-jama'ah*). They are brought in to indicate the dual and the plural, so they are established [in the word], and the marker of *raf'* comes upon the dual and the plural, while they already exist in them, so they are intended for it. Al-Sayyid 'Isa said: what is meant by their saying "every second [word] that takes *i'rab* ... etc." is "every second [word] that would take *i'rab* were it not already inflected." So ponder this and do not be heedless.

It is also permitted that ﴿yatazakka﴾ be with an implied *li-an yatazakka* ("in order that he may purify himself"), functioning as a causal clause (*'illah*) related to *yu'ti*. Then the *lam* was omitted, and the omission of the *lam* before *an* and *inna* is common. Then *an* was omitted, so the verb becomes *raf'* or remains in the accusative, as in the verse of Tarafah:

*Alā ayyuhādhā al-zājirī aḥḍura al-waghā*
(Ah, you who rebuke me, [saying], "Let me attend the battle")

It has been narrated with *raf'* of *aḥḍuru* and with its *nasb*. It was also said that it is with the implied *li-an* or *'an an* before *aḥḍura*, and it was treated in the same way as what you have heard. Whichever of these is the case, the discourse indicates that what is meant by giving it is spending it in the paths of righteousness and goodness.

And al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them all, read *yazzakkā* with the assimilation (*idghām*) of the *ta'* into the *zay*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verse 19:

﴿And there is not for anyone with Him any favor that is repaid.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) confirming what the preceding statement has conveyed, namely that his giving for the sake of purification (tazakki) is sincerely for the sake of God, the Exalted. That is: there is no one with whom He has a favor that is of the kind to be repaid and compensated, such that giving what is given would be intended as its recompense. It is known from what has been mentioned that the verb ﴿tujzā﴾ is in the passive voice (bināʾ li-l-mafʿūl), because the intention is not toward a specific agent. It has also been said that this is because it is a fāṣila (verse-ending rhyme), and its original form would be yujzaʾ bihi iyyāhā or yajziyhā iyyāhu.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verse 20:

﴿Except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High.﴾ It is in the accusative (manṣūb) as a disconnected exception (istithnā' munqaṭi', an exception not of the same kind as what precedes) from "a favour" (niʿma), because "seeking" is not included in it. The meaning is: rather, he did that seeking the countenance of his Lord, glorified is He, and desiring His good pleasure, mighty and majestic is He, and not in repayment of a favour.

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb recited "ibtighāʾu" (ابتغاءُ) in the nominative, as a substitute (badal) for the place (maḥall) of "min niʿma," since the nominative there is either as the subject (fāʿiliyya) or as the beginning of a sentence (ibtidā'), with "min" being superfluous (mazīda). The nominative in such a construction is the dialect of the Tamīm, and upon it is his (the poet's) saying:

*"And a land in which there is no companion, except the wild cattle, and except the camels."*

It is also related with both nominative and accusative, according to what is in al-Baḥr, the saying of Bishr ibn Abī Ḥāzim:

*"They have become empty wastes, with no companion in them, except the gazelles and the ostriches that roam about."*

It is also permissible that its accusative be as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu) according to the sense, because the meaning of the statement is that he gives his wealth for no reason among the reasons except for seeking the good pleasure of his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, and not in repayment of a favour. Thus it is an exception from the most general of causes and reasons (istithnā' mufarragh), and it was interpreted this way because the statement, I mean ﴿He gives his wealth﴾, is affirmative, whereas the exception that is omitted (mufarragh) is, according to the majority, restricted to negation. But when it is followed by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And for no one is there a favour to be repaid﴾, and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Will he not purify himself?﴾, including the negation of ostentation and reputation, it indicates the meaning mentioned.

Ibn Abī ʿAbla recited "ibtighā" (ابتغا) with the final vowel shortened (maqṣūr), and in it there is the possibility of both the accusative and the nominative.

These verses, as you have heard, were revealed concerning Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, because he used to free weak slaves, and his father said to him what he said, and he answered him with what he answered. I have already clarified what he, may Allah be pleased with him, left vague in his saying: "I only want what I want."

In the narration of Ibn Jarīr and Ibn ʿAsākir, he said: "O father, I only want what is with Allah, exalted is He." In the narration of ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him: he bought Bilāl, who was a slave of Umayya ibn Khalaf, who was torturing him for his Islam, for a ritl of gold, and freed him. The polytheists said: "Abū Bakr only freed him because of a favour that he had owed him." So this was revealed. And he, may Allah be pleased with him, was one of those who were tortured for their Islam, and the Ṣiddīq bought them and freed them.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from ʿUrwa that Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, freed seven, all of whom were being tortured for the sake of Allah, mighty and majestic is He: Bilāl, ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayra, al-Nahdiyya and her daughter, Zinnīra, Umm ʿUbays, and the slave-girl of the Banū al-Mu'ammil. And concerning him was revealed: ﴿And the most righteous will be kept away from it﴾, to the end of the surah.

The Imam used this as evidence that he, may Allah be pleased with him, is the most excellent of this Community. It was also mentioned that in these verses there is what refutes the saying of the Shīʿa that they were revealed concerning ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face. He extended the discussion on this and brought forward what is not free from dispute, and said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 92, verse 21:

His saying, Most High: ﴿And he will surely be satisfied﴾ is the response to an implied oath; that is, "By Allah, he will surely be satisfied." The pronoun in it refers to the most righteous (al-atqa) who was spoken of, and it is a generous promise of attaining all that he seeks in the most complete and most beautiful manner, since satisfaction (al-ridha) is realized through it. Imam (al-Razi) permitted that the pronoun refers to the Lord, Most High, saying after he had explained the sentence on the basis of its referring to al-atqa: "And in it, in my view, there is another aspect, namely that what is meant is that he spent only seeking the pleasure of Allah Most High, and ﴿and he will surely be satisfied﴾ means that Allah Most High will be pleased with him. And this, in my view, is greater than the first, because Allah's pleasure with His servant is more complete for the servant than his pleasure with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic." And in summary, both matters must occur, as He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾. End of quotation. The apparent meaning is the first, and it has been read as «wa-la-sawfa yurda» in the passive voice from the causative (al-irda'), and what he indicated regarding the meaning of ﴿well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ is not definitive, as you have heard. And in this sentence there is a discussion which will become clear from what comes shortly, God willing, Most High.
